title: Thoughts on the ending of “Taste of Cherry”?

commenti.body:
Your first sentence suggests that you're going to give some information about the movie without spoiling it, then you immediately give away the ending. Put a spoiler warning. Downvoted.

I think the ending is beautifully ambiguous. I remember reading that at first the last shot was supposed to be just him laying down in his grave but Kiarostami broke the fourth wall and showed the movie crews because he thought that the ending would have been too depressing and wanted to remind the audience that it was just fiction lest someone really depressed got affected otherwise. 

My own interpretation is that Mr. Baadi lived and found beauty in his life again. But you could also say that he dies and finds a peaceful afterlife he craved.

It's just very thoughtful and clever writing

I could kind of understand being sensitive to spoilers but Taste of Cherry is one of those films where getting spoilers doesn't affect anything at all. It's a film about a man trying to kill himself. Plot is the least of its concern. Even if you are spoiled it would still bring out a lot of emotions
It costs nothing to put a spoiler warning, and people who haven't seen the film can't distinguish between films that are okay to spoil and films that are not.
Why are you reading a post about the ending of a movie you haven’t seen and not expecting there to be spoilers?

One of the greatest movies I’ve ever seen…until it is RUINED by an utterly stupefying conceptual 180 degree turn at the end. I don’t understand this at all.

Come on. It´s Abbas Kiarostami, not some Marvel twist reveal stuff.
You gotta let this go for older films like this that aren't plot centric.

Kiarostami will go down in film history for his experimentation with artifice, incorporating himself in many of his films, using real people to play themselves, blurring the lines between documentary and narrative, making movies about the making of his movies, creating real live opportunities for reconciliation (however small) through his films, using the act of making a film to track down his child actors who potentially died in an earthquake. So much of his process is establishing a connective thread between the narrative of his film and the making of it. In a sense he is saying the story doesn’t stop after it fades to black. And while the central character may or may not have died, something of what he is connected to lives on. I think this conceptual approach is well suited way to get at a central theme in his work: what stops us from connecting with others? I wonder if you’d hate Felini’s Roma for similar injections of the process of filmmaking.
